title: Could online patient-reported outcome measures assess hand injury rehabilitation?
author: Kajitani, Liddy, et al.

steps.title: Prepare recruitment materials
steps.instruction: Print and assemble an invitation letter, an information sheet, and a consent form for each potential participant.

steps.title: Obtain consent and record injury
steps.instruction: After the participant signs the consent form, record the subject’s hand injury details on the HISS data acquisition sheet.

steps.title: Calculate Hand Injury Severity Score
steps.instruction: Use the recorded injury data to calculate the Hand Injury Severity Score (HISS), which will later be used as a variable in analyses.

steps.title: Distribute baseline questionnaire
steps.instruction: Provide the participant with the information sheet that contains a QR‑code; the QR‑code links to the baseline questionnaire hosted online.

steps.title: Collect general and demographic data
steps.instruction: In the baseline questionnaire, obtain identifiers (name, email) and demographic information (ethnicity, race, gender, age, hand dominance, occupation, education level, income).

steps.title: Administer Michigan Hand Outcomes Questionnaire
steps.instruction: Present the licensed Michigan Hand Outcomes Questionnaire (MHQ) in Google‑form format, covering the six domains (overall hand function, ADLs, pain, work performance, aesthetics, patient satisfaction) and the added items about number of rehabilitation sessions attended, therapist’s progress summary, and an optional question on pending court case.

steps.title: Schedule follow‑up questionnaires
steps.instruction: Email each participant links to follow‑up questionnaires at three post‑surgery intervals: 2–4 weeks, 6–8 weeks, and 10–14 weeks.

steps.title: Export questionnaire data securely
steps.instruction: Transfer all questionnaire responses to a password‑protected Excel file.

steps.title: Import data into statistical software
steps.instruction: Open the Excel file in IBM SPSS Statistics version 27.0 for analysis.

steps.title: Perform statistical analyses
steps.instruction: Analyze the data according to the following plan:

substeps.instruction: Report MHQ values as mean ± standard error.
Run multiple linear regression to test whether categorical variables (patient race, gender, injury severity) and numerical variables (patient age) predict MHQ scores.
Check regression assumptions: normality (Shapiro‑Wilk test and Q‑Q plots), homoscedasticity (Levene's test), multicollinearity (Variance Inflation Factors).
Compute Pearson correlation coefficients for relationships between continuous variables.
Conduct independent‑samples t‑tests to compare MHQ means between binary categorical variables.
Perform one‑way ANOVA for categorical variables with >2 groups (e.g., HISS severity categories: Minor, Moderate, Severe, Major).
Use repeated‑measures ANOVA to assess MHQ changes across the four time points (baseline, 2–4 weeks, 6–8 weeks, 10–14 weeks), applying Bonferroni post‑hoc tests when significant.
Report effect sizes: Cohen's d for t‑tests and partial eta‑squared for ANOVA.
Handle missing data with multiple imputation techniques.

Confirm sample‑size adequacy: a G*Power 3.1 power analysis indicated a minimum of 118 participants to detect a medium effect size (f² = 0.15) with α = 0.05 and 80 % power; the planned sample of 250 exceeds this requirement.

description: In this study, we aim to explore patient-reported outcomes (PROs) following hand trauma surgery by examining the factors that influence patient perceptions and how these perceptions evolve during rehabilitation. Introducing online versions of the MHQ and the HISS calculator might make these tools more accessible and convenient for patients, which could enhance data collection and improve rehabilitation strategies [8]. In selecting a Patient-Reported Outcome Measure (PROM), it is crucial to consider potential ceiling and floor effects to ensure the chosen outcome measures provide adequate precision and enable effective patient stratification. Shortened questionnaires like SF12 and Brief-MHQ, which use only one or two items to assess each domain, have been developed to address issues associated with longer questionnaires, such as incomplete data, lower response rates, and reduced quality of results due to responder fatigue and loss to follow-up [22]. However, there is limited research on the use of these shortened questionnaires to evaluate PROs following hand surgery. In contrast, longer questionnaires like the MHQ can capture the multidimensional aspects of a complex disease such as a hand injury. Rasch analysis has demonstrated that the MHQ is a reliable and valid measure for evaluating hand outcomes in older adults following treatment for distal radius fractures. This rigorous approach to questionnaire validation has been used to assess the psychometric properties of the MHQ in various conditions. However, results from Rasch analysis suggest that MHQ scores should be interpreted in a condition-specific manner, with a focus on individual domain scores rather than the summary MHQ score [23]. To address these issues, this study may employ Item Response Theory (IRT) via Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT) to model respondents' responses according to their level of function or ability.
